body:
`tests/autopilot/test_tick_lock.sh::test_the_fingerprint_actually_distinguishes_processes`
spawns a background `sleep`, waits `sleep 0.2`, then reads `_tick_lock_fingerprint "$pid"`.
Under load the process is not yet visible to `ps`, the fingerprint comes back empty, and both
that test and `test_a_recycled_pid_does_not_hold_the_lock_forever` fail.

Why this matters far more than a flaky test normally would: step 6 of
`scripts/autopilot-tick.sh` `exit 4`s on a red suite, deliberately, BEFORE phase-7. So a
transient flake stops the entire tick — no issue picked, nothing merged, no release train.

Measured 2026-08-08: the suite went red at load average 47-161 (an unrelated Xcode/simulator
build plus swap exhaustion — 28,976 MB of 29,696 MB used). The same probe succeeded 3/3 on
an idle shell, and the full suite reported 68 files / 0 failures once load fell to ~7.

This has already fired in production three times: `tick-tests-failed` on 2026-07-31,
2026-08-01 and 2026-08-05. Each cost a full tick of drainage.

Fix directions (not yet applied):
- poll for the pid to appear (retry `_tick_lock_fingerprint` until non-empty, bounded) rather
  than a fixed `sleep 0.2`; a fixed sleep can never be right on a machine whose load varies
  by two orders of magnitude
- and/or treat an empty fingerprint as "cannot determine" and skip the assertion rather than
  failing it, since the test's real subject is whether two DIFFERENT commands are
  distinguishable, not whether `ps` responded in time
- consider whether a red autopilot suite should really kill a tick outright, or whether the
  flake-prone subset should be quarantined so an infrastructure hiccup cannot stop drainage
title: Load-sensitive fingerprint flake in test_tick_lock.sh silently kills whole ticks
